```{=html}
<h2 class="research-section" id="jmp">Job Market Paper</h2>
<div class="paper-entry no-image" data-paper>
<div class="paper-body">
<h3 class="paper-title"><a href="research/bias-reduction-tstsls.html">Bias Reduction in TSTSLS Applications: A Quantile Adjustment Method</a></h3>
<div class="paper-venue">Latest version: October 2026</div>
<p class="paper-abstract"><span data-abstract-short>Many research questions require income and a second variable measured for the same people, but the two are often recorded in separate samples. Two-sample two-stage (TSTS) imputation bridges the samples by predicting income from characteristics both record.</span><span data-abstract-full hidden>Many research questions require income and a second variable measured for the same people, but the two are often recorded in separate samples. Two-sample two-stage (TSTS) imputation bridges the samples by predicting income from characteristics both record. However, the predictions are less dispersed than actual income, and they miss any link between income and the second variable that the shared characteristics do not capture. Existing corrections fix these problems one at a time, and fixing only the first can make an estimate worse. I propose a quantile adjustment that replaces each prediction with the observed income at the same rank. It restores the income distribution and, in the same step, shifts the covariance with the second variable. I characterise when this shift helps and provide two diagnostics. In applications to Mexico, Ecuador and Chile, the adjustment comes closest to the full-sample benchmark on 14 of 19 estimands and within 0.6 percentage points of the best method on the other 5.</span> <button type="button" class="abstract-more" data-toggle-abstract aria-expanded="false">Read more <i class="bi bi-chevron-down"></i></button></p>

<h3 class="paper-title">Inequality of Opportunity in Mexico and its Regions: A Data-Driven Approach</h3>
<div class="paper-venue"><a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/00220388.2022.2055465">The Journal of Development Studies (2022)</a>, <em>with Thibaut Plassot and Isidro Soloaga</em></div>
<p class="paper-abstract"><span data-abstract-short>This research proposes a first approximation of Inequality of Opportunity (IOp) in Mexico based on a concept of ex-post compensation, fully consistent with Roemer’s approach.</span><span data-abstract-full hidden>This research proposes a first approximation of Inequality of Opportunity (IOp) in Mexico based on a concept of ex-post compensation, fully consistent with Roemer’s approach. This framework considers the advantage reached by an individual to be determined by the circumstances and by the effort exerted. Following Brunori and Neidhöfer, we construct a data-driven procedure using regression trees to identify types based on circumstances. To identify effort, an algorithm estimates the distribution of outcome in each type based on coefficients of Bernstein polynomials. We present IOp indicators for both an ex-ante and an ex-post approach. Our results underline the differences, in terms of opportunities, faced by individuals, based on the territory in which they grew up, the household context, and personal characteristics. The education and the wealth of parents, and the area of residence at age of 14 are the principal circumstances that shape the trajectories, besides the skin tone or the region. Importantly, territorial variables are significant among the individuals in relative poor households at age of 14, but they hold less importance for the others. IOp is higher in rural areas, in the South and in the Center compared to other regions.</span> <button type="button" class="abstract-more" data-toggle-abstract aria-expanded="false">Read more <i class="bi bi-chevron-down"></i></button></p>

<h3 class="paper-title">Brechas salariales por autoidentificación indígena y rasgos lingüísticos en México</h3>
<div class="other-en">Wage gaps due to indigenous self-identification and linguistic traits in Mexico</div>
<div class="paper-venue"><a href="https://doi.org/10.48102/rsm.vi3.94">Sobre México. Temas de Economía (2021)</a>, <em>with Eva O. Arceo-Gómez</em></div>
<p class="paper-abstract"><span data-abstract-short>Mexico is a highly unequal country, and ethno-racial origin is one of the dimensions contributing to this inequality. Previous studies have analyzed wage differences by ethno-racial origin and linguistic traits.</span><span data-abstract-full hidden>Mexico is a highly unequal country, and ethno-racial origin is one of the dimensions contributing to this inequality. Previous studies have analyzed wage differences by ethno-racial origin and linguistic traits. Still, so far, no study has recognized that indigenous self-identification can lead to selection biases in the analysis. In this article, we solve this problem by estimating a switching regression model, which in a first stage estimates the selection in self-identification, and in a second stage, two wage equations according to how the worker self-identified. The model reveals that most of the difference in average wages between those who identify as indigenous and those who do not is due to selection bias. Despite this, an unexplained differential persists (unexplained by observed characteristics or self-selection), which could be due to discrimination. These results contrast with traditional Oaxaca decompositions in which selection bias is not considered and suggest that education is the factor that contributes the most to ethnic-racial wage inequality.</span> <button type="button" class="abstract-more" data-toggle-abstract aria-expanded="false">Read more <i class="bi bi-chevron-down"></i></button></p>

<h3 class="paper-title">Global Estimates of Opportunity and Mobility: A Database</h3>
<div class="paper-venue"><a href="https://researchonline.lse.ac.uk/id/eprint/130992/">Stone Center Working Paper (2026)</a>, <em>with 17 co-authors</em><br><em>Coordinated by Francisco H.G. Ferreira, Vito Peragine, Paolo Brunori and Pedro Salas-Rojo</em></div>
<p class="paper-abstract"><span data-abstract-short>This paper describes a new public-access online database containing internationally comparable estimates of inequality of opportunity for seventy-two countries, covering two-thirds of the world’s population.</span><span data-abstract-full hidden>This paper describes a new public-access online database containing internationally comparable estimates of inequality of opportunity for seventy-two countries, covering two-thirds of the world’s population. The estimates were computed directly from the unit-record microdata for 196 household surveys, using a suite of machine-learning tools selected to minimize the omitted variable and overfitting biases discussed in the literature. Overall, differences in opportunities account for substantial shares of total income inequality (with the mean of our preferred estimate being 40.9%), but there is substantial variation across countries, with estimates ranging from 18.9% in Denmark (2011) to 76.7% in South Africa (2017). The latest US estimate of 41.6% places it among the most opportunity-unequal high-income countries. We also find strong support for the existence of a positive association between income inequality and relative inequality of opportunity, analogous to the “Great Gatsby Curve” for mobility and inequality. Similarly, there is evidence of an inverted-U “Opportunity Kuznets curve”. The database is available at www.geom.ecineq.org.</span> <button type="button" class="abstract-more" data-toggle-abstract aria-expanded="false">Read more <i class="bi bi-chevron-down"></i></button></p>

<h3 class="paper-title">Survey-to-Survey Imputation When External Covariates Matter: Estimating Inequality of Opportunity in Mexico</h3>
<div class="paper-venue"><a href="https://ceey.org.mx/survey-to-survey-imputation-when-external-covariates-matter-estimating-inequality-of-opportunity-in-mexico/">CEEY Working Paper (2025)</a>, <em>with Luis A. Monroy-Gómez-Franco and Roberto Vélez-Grajales</em></div>
<p class="paper-abstract"><span data-abstract-short>Accurate measurement of income and consumption is essential for understanding socioeconomic disparities and informing effective policy interventions. However, survey data often lack comprehensive income or consumption data.</span><span data-abstract-full hidden>Accurate measurement of income and consumption is essential for understanding socioeconomic disparities and informing effective policy interventions. However, survey data often lack comprehensive income or consumption data. Researchers typically employ asset-based indices or survey-to-survey imputation techniques to address this limitation. While these methods provide valuable insights, they can introduce biases, particularly when the analysis involves covariates not used in the prediction process. This paper proposes a novel imputation methodology that aims to mitigate these biases. Our approach focuses on preserving individuals’ relative positions within the income distribution while introducing variance. This ensures that the underlying rank order of individuals is maintained, addressing a common shortcoming of existing imputation techniques. Through rigorous validation and comparison, we demonstrate the robustness and effectiveness of our proposed method using the ENIGH survey in Mexico. To illustrate one practical application of our approach, we analyze inequality of opportunity, imputing income from the ENIGH into the ESRU-EMOVI survey. Our findings underscore the importance of carefully considering imputation methods in socioeconomic research. We demonstrate that traditional imputation procedures can lead to downward-biased estimates of inequality of opportunity compared to our proposed method.</span> <button type="button" class="abstract-more" data-toggle-abstract aria-expanded="false">Read more <i class="bi bi-chevron-down"></i></button></p>

<h3 class="paper-title">Follow the Leader? Public health messaging and containment of mobility during a pandemic</h3>
<div class="paper-venue"><a href="https://www.undp.org/latin-america/publications/follow-leader-public-health-messaging-and-containment-mobility-during-pandemic">UNDP Working Paper (2022)</a>, <em>with Sandra Aguilar-Gómez, Eva O. Arceo-Gómez and Elia De la Cruz Toledo</em></div>
<p class="paper-abstract"><span data-abstract-short>The effectiveness of widespread policy measures during the COVID-19 pandemic hinges upon compliance with ordinances. This study explores how leaders’ discourse relates to compliance with stay-at-home orders to mitigate the spread of COVID-19 in Mexico.</span><span data-abstract-full hidden>The effectiveness of widespread policy measures during the COVID-19 pandemic hinges upon compliance with ordinances. This study explores how leaders’ discourse relates to compliance with stay-at-home orders to mitigate the spread of COVID-19 in Mexico. It uses municipality-level mobility data from geolocation events of smartphone users and daily briefings from the President and the coronavirus czar. Quantile regressions, sentiment analysis and topic modelling are used to shed light on the dynamics between political discourse and containment of mobility. Discrepancies were found between the content and tone of the President and those of the coronavirus czar. These contrasts translate into differences in the association between the content of the speeches and mobility patterns. The discourse’s association with mobility is mediated by awareness of COVID-19-related topics and by individuals’ political affiliation.</span> <button type="button" class="abstract-more" data-toggle-abstract aria-expanded="false">Read more <i class="bi bi-chevron-down"></i></button></p>

<h3 class="paper-title">New Echoes of Deep Mexico? Indigenous Identity and Its Enduring Imprints</h3>
<div class="paper-venue"><a href="https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6238198">in <em>Roots of Underdevelopment: A New Economic (and Political) History of Latin America and the Caribbean, Volume 2</em> (2026)</a>, <em>with L. Guillermo Woo-Mora</em><br><em>Edited by Felipe Valencia Caicedo</em></div>
<p class="paper-abstract"><span data-abstract-short>This chapter revisits Guillermo Bonfil Batalla's &quot;México Profundo&quot; (1987) through the lens of contemporary empirical historical economics. In that work, Bonfil Batalla argued that beneath a Westernized facade of modern Mexico lies a &quot;Deep Mexico&quot;: a living but denied Indigenous…</span><span data-abstract-full hidden>This chapter revisits Guillermo Bonfil Batalla's &quot;México Profundo&quot; (1987) through the lens of contemporary empirical historical economics. In that work, Bonfil Batalla argued that beneath a Westernized facade of modern Mexico lies a &quot;Deep Mexico&quot;: a living but denied Indigenous civilization that continues to shape the country's culture, identity, and social life. The first part of the chapter compiles historical census tabulations and harmonized microdata to document persistent patterns of Indigenous identity, inequality, and historical continuity. The historical process of Indigenous identification is multidimensional and endogenous, shaped by language, self-identification, phenotype, and geography. Despite improvements in basic services, Indigenous populations continue to face structural gaps in education and income. Beyond explicit identifiers, the second part of the chapter examines three channels through which &quot;México Profundo&quot; continues to influence economic life. First, skin tone remains a consistent predictor of disadvantage, reflecting racialized inequality. Second, historical Indigenous presence structures spatial inequality and human-capital outcomes. Third, Indigenous institutions, both formal and informal, continue to shape development trajectories, depending on their interaction with markets and the state. Together, these patterns underscore that &quot;México Profundo&quot; continues to illuminate key mechanisms linking Indigenous identity to economic and social outcomes in modern Mexico.</span> <button type="button" class="abstract-more" data-toggle-abstract aria-expanded="false">Read more <i class="bi bi-chevron-down"></i></button></p>
<div class="paper-buttons"><a class="pill" href="https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6238198" target="_blank"><i class="bi bi-file-earmark-text"></i>Paper</a>

<h2 class="research-section" id="work-in-progress">Work in Progress</h2>
<div class="paper-entry no-image" data-paper>
<div class="paper-body">
<h3 class="paper-title">Estimating Intergenerational Mobility: A Machine Learning Approach</h3>
<p class="paper-abstract"><span data-abstract-short>Transition matrices are a central tool in intergenerational mobility research, yet existing estimation methods face a tension that no single approach resolves.</span><span data-abstract-full hidden>Transition matrices are a central tool in intergenerational mobility research, yet existing estimation methods face a tension that no single approach resolves. Fully non-parametric methods break down under data constraints and cannot produce coherent comparisons across demographic groups; parametric alternatives impose functional form restrictions that may distort estimated mobility patterns. I develop the positional functions framework, which estimates a complete probability distribution over all possible income destinations for each individual, conditional on parental position and observable characteristics. Aggregating these individual distributions yields transition matrices that are fully non-parametric, incorporate covariates directly, and decompose exactly into subpopulation components, so that observed differences across groups reflect mobility heterogeneity rather than methodological artifacts. Using Swedish administrative data covering 1.3 million father-offspring pairs, I show that the framework recovers the same mobility patterns as established methods when data are abundant and outperforms them in the tails of the distribution, where poverty traps and elite reproduction are most salient. It also maintains coherent subpopulation comparisons even when group sizes differ dramatically.</span> <button type="button" class="abstract-more" data-toggle-abstract aria-expanded="false">Read more <i class="bi bi-chevron-down"></i></button></p>
</div>
</div>
<div class="paper-entry no-image" data-paper>
<div class="paper-body">
<h3 class="paper-title">From Rags to Riches? The Impact of Education Reform on Intergenerational Social Mobility in Mexico</h3>
<p class="paper-abstract"><span data-abstract-short>This study examines the impact of educational expansion on intergenerational mobility through a quasi-experiment created by a Mexican education reform of the early 1990s. In a significant educational reform, Mexico extended the mandatory years of schooling in the summer of 1993.</span><span data-abstract-full hidden>This study examines the impact of educational expansion on intergenerational mobility through a quasi-experiment created by a Mexican education reform of the early 1990s. In a significant educational reform, Mexico extended the mandatory years of schooling in the summer of 1993. By using retrospective data on parental and individual socioeconomic status, this research employs a sharp regression discontinuity design to assess whether the reform had short- or long-term effects on intergenerational mobility outcomes. The findings indicate no immediate effect of the reform, though there is a potential long-term effect evident in the improvement of trends related to intergenerational outcomes.</span> <button type="button" class="abstract-more" data-toggle-abstract aria-expanded="false">Read more <i class="bi bi-chevron-down"></i></button></p>
</div>
</div>

```
